page.title: IPLA under a logarithmic Sobolev inequality: proofs and sources
page.heading: IPLA under a log-Sobolev inequality
page.subtitle: Joint relative-entropy convergence for the particle algorithm through scaled Gaussian Euler laws.
page.description: Particle relative-entropy estimates under a lifted-target logarithmic Sobolev inequality, gradient smoothness, and finite initial joint entropy.
page.status: The particle entropy theorem follows from gradient smoothness, a logarithmic Sobolev inequality for the lifted Gibbs law, an admissible positive step, and finite initial joint entropy. Gaussian density regularity, entropy differentiation, moment estimates, and compatibility of constants are derived.

intro:
Scaling the latent coordinates identifies IPLA with Gaussian Euler for its summed particle potential. The entropy argument for Gaussian Euler then gives the particle estimate under a logarithmic Sobolev inequality for the lifted Gibbs target and finite initial joint entropy. The Gaussian density, entropy derivative, initial-time bound, score moments, and constant compatibility are established in that argument.

The conditional interpolation-data statements are also recorded with their additional analytic premises. Their source declarations and anchors are retained. Those premises belong to the conditional results and are not added to the finite-initial-entropy theorem.

sections.title: Entropy convergence from a lifted-target logarithmic Sobolev inequality
sections.intro: The theorem assumes gradient smoothness, the lifted-target logarithmic Sobolev inequality, a positive admissible step, and finite initial joint entropy. Gaussian interpolation supplies the analytic regularity and required moments. Each conclusion includes finite output divergence before its ordinary numerical estimate is stated.

steps.title: Finite joint entropy and the particle estimate
steps.body:
Let \(N>0\), \(D=d_\theta+Nd_x\), and \(V_N(z)=\sum_iU(\theta,\sqrt N z_i)\). Assume \(U\) is differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, a logarithmic Sobolev inequality of constant \(\beta>0\) holds for the lifted Gibbs target \(\Pi_N\), and a positive step obeys \(\gamma\le\beta/(4NL^2)\). Let initial joint entropy \(H_0\) be finite. Then every particle law has finite divergence and

\[H_k\le e^{-\beta\gamma k/N}H_0+\frac{8\gamma ND L^2}{\beta}.\]

The lifted gradient has constant \(NL\) and its Gaussian Euler law at \(h=\gamma/N\) equals the particle law. The restriction is equivalent to \(h\le\beta/(4(NL)^2)\), so the entropy theorem applies with \(h=\gamma/N\), dimension \(D\), and gradient constant \(NL\). Substitution gives rate \(e^{-\beta\gamma k/N}\) and error \(8\gamma ND L^2/\beta\). The admissible positive step also gives positive \(L\) before division. Gaussian interpolation regularity and compatibility are derived, rather than added as separate premises.

steps.title: The entropy bound divided by particle count
steps.body:
Divide the finite joint inequality by positive \(N\):

\[\frac{H_k}{N}\le e^{-\beta\gamma k/N}\frac{H_0}{N}+\frac{8\gamma D L^2}{\beta}.\]

Every term, including the initial entropy, is divided by the same particle count. One factor cancels from the error term. Finiteness remains a statement about the full joint divergence. The divided quantity is not the parameter-marginal entropy, which is obtained separately by data processing.

steps.title: Linear scaling of the lifted logarithmic Sobolev constant
steps.body:
Suppose the lifted target has constant \(\beta=N\alpha\) with \(\alpha>0\). Positive particle count gives \(\beta>0\), and condition \(\gamma\le\beta/(4NL^2)\) is equivalent to \(\gamma\le\alpha/(4L^2)\). Substitution in the normalized theorem gives rate \(e^{-\alpha\gamma k}\). The dimension relation \(D/N=d_x+d_\theta/N\) makes the error term \((8\gamma L^2/\alpha)(d_x+d_\theta/N)\), yielding

\[\frac{H_k}{N}\le e^{-\alpha\gamma k}\frac{H_0}{N}+\frac{8\gamma L^2}{\alpha}\left(d_x+\frac{d_\theta}{N}\right).\]

The functional inequality is assumed for \(\Pi_N\) itself, and the finite-divergence conclusion is retained. The shared parameter prevents inference of this constant merely by independent tensorization of pair models.

steps.title: The parameter-law divergence estimate
steps.body:
Project the particle and reference laws by the same measurable parameter map. Data processing gives \(\operatorname{KL}(\mu_k^\theta\Vert\Pi_N^\theta)\le H_k\). The joint theorem supplies \(H_k<\infty\), so projected divergence is finite. Substitution yields

\[\operatorname{KL}(\mu_k^\theta\Vert\Pi_N^\theta)\le e^{-\beta\gamma k/N}H_0+\frac{8\gamma ND L^2}{\beta}.\]

The initial term remains full joint entropy \(H_0\), and the unnormalized error retains factor \(N\). A bound on joint entropy per particle must be multiplied by \(N\) before bounding this ordinary parameter divergence.

sections.title: Conditional estimates with regular interpolation data
sections.intro: A conditional theorem is also available when relative-density interpolation, weak-equation, differentiability, and energy data are already supplied. Its assumptions are recorded below. The separate Gaussian theorem derives those properties from finite initial entropy and the stated potential and target conditions.

steps.title: The conditional full joint entropy estimate
steps.body:
Let \(N>0\) and nonnegative dimensions \(d_\theta,d_x\). Assume differentiable \(U:\mathbb R^{d_\theta+d_x}\to\mathbb R\) has \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient and put \(D=d_\theta+Nd_x\). Let \(\Pi_N\) be the normalized Gibbs law of \(V_N\) and \(\mu_k\) the scaled Gaussian particle law. Define

\[ H_k=\operatorname{KL}(\mu_k\Vert\Pi_N). \]

Assume initial probability \(\mu_0\) and a logarithmic Sobolev inequality for \(\Pi_N\) with constant \(\beta>0\), together with

\[ \beta\le NL,\qquad 0<\gamma\le\frac{\beta}{4NL^2}. \]

In this conditional theorem also assume the regular relative-density interpolation for potential \(V_N\), constant \(\beta\), step \(\gamma/N\), gradient constant \(NL\), and initial law \(\mu_0\). The data contain the density representation, weak equation, differentiability, integrability, and error estimates described below. They imply finiteness of \(H_k\) for every \(k\) and

\[ H_k\le e^{-\beta\gamma k/N}H_0 +\frac{8\gamma ND L^2}{\beta}. \]

Positivity of \(L\) follows from \(\beta>0\) and \(\beta\le NL\). Compatibility \(\beta\le NL\) is an explicit premise here. In positive dimension the separate Gaussian interpolation theorem derives it and the needed regularity from its own hypotheses; the singleton case is treated directly. Neither theorem in this entropy argument assumes strong convexity.

steps.title: The conditional per-particle entropy estimate
steps.body:
For the conditional theorem with regular interpolation data, divide the full estimate by positive particle count and define \(\overline H_k=H_k/N\). Then

\[ \overline H_k\le e^{-\beta\gamma k/N}\overline H_0 +\frac{8\gamma D L^2}{\beta}. \]

Both the initial contribution and error are divided by \(N\), preserving order. This remains entropy of the entire state divided by \(N\). To bound unnormalized parameter divergence, undo this division before using data processing. For fixed nonzero step the additive error need not vanish, and the result does not assert invariance of \(\Pi_N\) under the Euler transition.

sections.title: The scaled potential and physical particle update
sections.intro: Scaling the latent coordinates identifies the particle potential and Gaussian transition with a Euclidean Euler problem. The following coordinate equalities determine the dimension, gradient constant, step, and two physical noise amplitudes used in the entropy estimate.

steps.title: The scaled state and lifted Gibbs target
steps.body:
Write \(z=(\theta,z^1,\ldots,z^N)\) and physical latent coordinates \(x^i=\sqrt N\,z^i\). Define

\[ V_N(z)=\sum_{i=1}^N U(\theta,\sqrt N\,z^i),\qquad \Pi_N(dz)=Z_N^{-1}e^{-V_N(z)}\,dz. \]

The potential \(V_N\) is the sum of the original pair potentials at these physical coordinates. The parameter is unchanged, and the state dimension is \(D=d_\theta+Nd_x\). Thus the parameter and latent dimensions \(d_\theta\) and \(d_x\) may differ.

The logarithmic Sobolev assumption includes normalization of this lifted target. The density expression alone would not establish a positive finite partition. The hypothesis concerns the full lifted law and is not replaced by a functional inequality for a single pair.

steps.title: The Gaussian recursion in physical coordinates
steps.body:
Gaussian Euler for \(V_N\) with \(h=\gamma/N\) has update

\[ z_{k+1}=z_k-\frac\gamma N\nabla V_N(z_k) +\sqrt{\frac{2\gamma}{N}}\,\xi_k, \qquad\xi_k\sim\mathcal N(0,I_D). \]

The parameter derivative of \(V_N\) sums the pair parameter gradients, and latent derivative \(i\) is \(\sqrt N\,\nabla_x U(\theta,\sqrt N z^i)\). Multiplying the scaled latent equation by the square root of particle count gives

\[ \theta_{k+1}=\theta_k-\frac\gamma N\sum_{i=1}^N \nabla_\theta U(\theta_k,x_k^i) +\sqrt{\frac{2\gamma}{N}}\,\xi_k^\theta, \]\[ x_{k+1}^i=x_k^i-\gamma\nabla_x U(\theta_k,x_k^i) +\sqrt{2\gamma}\,\xi_k^i. \]

These are coordinate identities, including the distinct parameter and latent noise coefficients. The scalar innovation coordinates are independent at all coordinates and times, and the whole sequence is independent of initialization. Those explicit distribution assumptions identify the supplied recursion with this transition.

steps.title: The lifted gradient Lipschitz constant
steps.body:
Let \(J_i z=(\theta,\sqrt N z^i)\). Orthogonality and repeated occurrence of the common parameter give

\[ \sum_{i=1}^N\|J_i v\|^2=N\|v\|^2. \]

The chain rule yields \( \langle\nabla V_N(z),v\rangle =\sum_i\langle\nabla U(J_i z),J_i v\rangle \). Apply the \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient bound to a difference, and Cauchy–Schwarz over particles. Applying the norm identity to both arguments gives

\[ \|\nabla V_N(z)-\nabla V_N(w)\| \le NL\,\|z-w\|. \]

Differentiability and this constant for \(V_N\) follow from the pair assumptions on \(U\). The logarithmic Sobolev constant \(\beta\) is a separate hypothesis about the target.

Indeed each pair norm contributes \(\|v_\theta\|^2\) in its parameter part and \(N\|v_i\|^2\) in its latent part, summing to \(N\|v_\theta\|^2+N\sum_i\|v_i\|^2=N\|v\|^2\). The directional gradient difference is bounded by

\[ L\Big(\sum_i\|J_i(z-w)\|^2\Big)^{1/2} \Big(\sum_i\|J_i v\|^2\Big)^{1/2} =NL\|z-w\|\,\|v\|. \]

Taking the unit-direction supremum gives the claimed constant. The scaled coordinates are the Euclidean metric in which the particle transition has isotropic Gaussian noise.

sections.title: The Gaussian transition laws and recursion
sections.intro: The iterated Gaussian probability kernel and a noise-driven recursion are two representations of the same finite-time laws. Measurability and the complete innovation-sequence distribution establish their equality.

steps.title: Gaussian transition iteration and probability preservation
steps.body:
Define the law after \(k\) iterations of the Gaussian Euler transition for \(V_N\) at step \(\gamma/N\) starting from \(\mu\). At \(k=0\) it is \(\mu\). Each next law pushes the product of its current law and the standard \(D\)-dimensional Gaussian through the update map.

Gradient Lipschitzness gives measurability, so every iterate is a probability measure. This definition starts directly from a measure, without choosing a particular random-variable realization. The frozen-drift interpolation started at \(\mu_k\) has law \(\mu_k\) at zero and \(\mu_{k+1}\) at \(h=\gamma/N\). These exact interval-boundary laws make the continuous entropy inequality a discrete recurrence.

steps.title: Equality with a supplied Gaussian particle realization
steps.body:
Take an \(L^2\) initialization and \(L^2\) innovation vectors. Assume each scalar innovation has law \(\mathcal N(0,1)\), all scalar coordinates at all times are mutually independent, and the sequence is independent of initialization. The complete input law is then determined by the initial pushforward and the Gaussian product law.

The measurable recursion therefore has the same law as the iterated Gaussian transition at every finite time. Substitution transfers the conditional normalized entropy theorem and its linear-constant specialization, retaining the regular interpolation hypotheses. This also identifies the finite-initial-entropy theorem with the same recursion when its hypotheses hold.

The random-variable formulation uses an \(L^2\) initial state, while the measure formulation starts from an initial probability law. Neither requires Gaussian initialization. Equality of their output laws, rather than an assumed error estimate, connects the two descriptions.

sections.title: The conditional interpolation assumptions and their consequences
sections.intro: The conditional theorem assumes regular relative-density interpolation, including the weak equation and full local time regularity. The Gaussian theorem instead proves positive-time absolute continuity using bounded entropy tests and controls the initial time by an explicit one-sided entropy majorant. This avoids adding the conditional structure’s two-sided initial-time regularity as a premise.

steps.title: The relative-density functional inequality and conditional interpolation assumptions
steps.body:
Write \( u=\Pi_N\), \(\ell=NL\), and \(h=\gamma/N\). The logarithmic Sobolev convention is

\[ 2 eta\operatorname{KL}(r u\Vert u) \le \int\| abla\log r\|^2\,d(r u). \]

The test class consists of positive \(C^1\) relative densities normalized as probabilities. Extension to all densities by approximation is not part of this definition.

The conditional interpolation assumptions give densities \(r_k(t,z)\), time derivatives \(\dot r_k(t,z)\), and error fields \(e_k(t,z)\). For \(0\le t\le h\), measure \(r_k(t) u\) is the frozen-drift Gaussian law started from iteration \(k\). The density is positive and spatially \(C^1\); local time regularity includes measurable pointwise derivatives and integrable domination for differentiation of \(r\log r\).

Also assume finite relative-score and error energies and a measurable mixed term. The weak identity holds for \(0\le t

steps.title: Entropy dissipation from the conditional weak equation
steps.body:
For each \(C^1\) test \(\psi\) with the required integrability, the weak identity is

\[ \int\dot r\,\psi\,d u =-\int\langle abla r, abla\psi angle\,d u +\int r\langle e, abla\psi angle\,d u. \]

Its last sign fixes the convention for \(e\). For a frozen drift the field has intended form \(e(z)= abla V_N(z)-\mathbb E[ abla V_N(X_0)\mid X_t=z]\). This conditional result assumes the weak identity for such a field; the Gaussian construction instead derives an integrable kernel flux and passes bounded logarithmic tests to the entropy identity.

Local domination justifies differentiation of entropy. Substitute \(1+\log r\), use \( abla r=r abla\log r\), and apply \(\langle e,s angle\le\|s\|^2/4+\|e\|^2\). With \(J(t)=\int\| abla\log r\|^2d(r u)\) this gives

\[ H'(t)\le- frac34 J(t)+\int r(t,z)\|e(t,z)\|^2\, u(dz). \]

The derivative estimate therefore follows from the density, weak-equation, and integrability assumptions. It is not a separate assumed entropy derivative.

steps.title: The error and score energies and finite entropy
steps.body:
The conditional interpolation assumptions include

\[\int r_k(t)\|e_k(t)\|^2d\nu\le t^2\ell^2G_k+2tD\ell^2,\qquad G_k\le\frac{4\ell^2}{\beta}H_k+2D\ell.\]

For the Gaussian interpolation these estimates are derived. Independence and Gaussian centering give \(\mathbb E\|Y_t-X\|^2=t^2G_k+2tD\), and gradient Lipschitzness multiplies this displacement moment by \(\ell^2\). Its kernel pair-law representation gives the corresponding spatial error energy.

Gaussian averaging of the Gibbs score exponential bound and the entropy variational inequality yield \(G_k\le4\ell H_k+2D\ell\) with integrability. Compatibility \(\beta\le\ell\) then yields coefficient \(4\ell^2/\beta\). No entropy–transport theorem is needed. Positive-time Gaussian Fisher information and the target functional inequality prove finite next entropy. Thus the unconditional theorem derives these analytic inputs from finite initial entropy, whereas the conditional theorem retains them as explicit interpolation premises.

sections.title: The one-step recurrence and particle scaling
sections.intro: The Gaussian Euler argument derives the entropy recurrence from the functional inequality and error-energy bounds. Substitution of the lifted potential, scaled time, gradient constant, and dimension then gives the particle coefficients by exact algebra.

steps.title: The conditional one-step entropy inequality
steps.body:
Combine the entropy derivative estimate with \(2\beta H(t)\le J(t)\). On \(0\le t\[ H'(t)\le-\tfrac32\beta H(t)+t^2\ell^2G_k+2tD\ell^2. \]

The restrictions \(h\le\beta/(4\ell^2)\) and \(\beta\le\ell\) imply \(h\ell\le1/4\) and \(\beta h\le1/4\). Bound the initial score moment by \(G_k\le A\) with \(A=(4\ell^2/\beta)H_k+2D\ell\). Then

\[ H'(t)\le-\tfrac32\beta H(t)+b, \qquad b=\tfrac\beta4 H_k+\tfrac52 hD\ell^2. \]

The integrating-factor estimate bounds the forcing by \(bh\). Inequality \(e^{-3x/2}+x/4\le e^{-x}\) for \(0\le x\le1/4\), multiplied by nonnegative \(H_k\) at \(x=\beta h\), includes the old-entropy forcing in the weaker exponential factor. Using \(5/2\le6\) gives

\[ H_{k+1}\le e^{-\beta h}H_k+6h^2D\ell^2. \]

More explicitly \(h^2\ell^2(4\ell^2/\beta)\le\beta/4\) follows from \(h\ell^2\le\beta/4\). Also \(2h^2D\ell^3\le hD\ell^2/2\) follows from \(h\ell\le1/4\). Adding noise term \(2hD\ell^2\) gives coefficient \(5/2\) in \(b\). Nonnegative \(H_k\) and dimension justify these multiplications. Integration bounds the total forcing by \(bh\). These quantitative steps derive the recurrence from the stated interpolation assumptions.

steps.title: The particle-scaled step and forcing
steps.body:
Under positive particle count and the stated denominator conditions, the step equivalence is

\[ \frac\gamma N\le\frac\beta{4(NL)^2} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \gamma\le\frac\beta{4NL^2}. \]

The forcing identity is

\[ 6\left(\frac\gamma N\right)^2D(NL)^2 =6\gamma^2DL^2. \]

Hence the particle joint law satisfies \(H_{k+1}\le e^{-\beta\gamma/N}H_k+6\gamma^2DL^2\). Division by positive \(N\) gives

\[ \overline H_{k+1}\le e^{-\beta\gamma/N}\overline H_k +\frac{6\gamma^2DL^2}{N}. \]

The interpolation theorem derives the joint recurrence and then this normalized form. A scalar normalization statement may instead assume a recurrence and divide it; that algebra alone does not prove the recurrence for a probability transition.

steps.title: The finite geometric sum and coefficient eight
steps.body:
For \(q=e^{-\beta h}\), induction gives

\[ H_k\le q^kH_0+6h^2D\ell^2\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}q^j. \]

Under \(0<\beta h\le1/4\), bound \(1-e^{-\beta h}\ge3\beta h/4\) makes the sum at most \(4/(3\beta h)\) and gives error term \(8hD\ell^2/\beta\). The lifted substitutions are

\[ e^{-\beta hk}=e^{-\beta\gamma k/N},\qquad \frac{8hD\ell^2}{\beta}=\frac{8\gamma ND L^2}{\beta}. \]

Dividing full entropy by \(N\) cancels the corresponding factor in the error. The coefficient \(8\) is inherited from the scalar Gaussian Euler estimate; every power of \(N\) follows from the coordinate and time scalings above. The finite-sum version remains valid at each finite iteration.

sections.title: The additional constant scaling \(\beta=N\alpha\)
sections.intro: Suppose the logarithmic Sobolev constant of the lifted Gibbs target is \(N\alpha\). This additional target property simplifies the physical step restriction and rate. It is not inferred from a functional inequality for one parameter–latent pair.

steps.title: The step and rate under a linearly scaled lifted constant
steps.body:
The additional hypothesis is that the coupled lifted target has logarithmic Sobolev constant \(N\alpha\). Suppose \(\alpha>0\), \(\alpha\le L\), and target \(\Pi_N\) has constant \(\beta=N\alpha\). Positive-denominator algebra gives

\[ N\alpha\le NL\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \alpha\le L, \qquad \gamma\le\frac{N\alpha}{4NL^2} \ \Longleftrightarrow\ \gamma\le\frac\alpha{4L^2}. \]

The exponent is \(e^{-(N\alpha)\gamma k/N}=e^{-\alpha\gamma k}\). These cancellations use \(N>0\). In positive dimension compatibility follows from the target functional inequality and gradient smoothness; on a singleton every divergence is zero.

The decay coefficient is uniform in \(N\) only because the lifted constant grows linearly with \(N\). With a fixed lower bound on \(\beta\), the general exponent remains \(\beta\gamma/N\) and the physical step restriction retains its particle dependence. The linear scaling is therefore an additional target property, not an independent-pair tensorization consequence.

steps.title: The dimension and error terms per particle
steps.body:
The normalized error satisfies

\[ \frac DN=d_x+\frac{d_\theta}{N},\qquad \frac{8\gamma DL^2}{N\alpha} =\frac{8\gamma L^2}{\alpha} \left(d_x+\frac{d_\theta}{N}\right). \]

Substitution in the normalized theorem gives

\[ \overline H_k\le e^{-\alpha\gamma k}\overline H_0 +\frac{8\gamma L^2}{\alpha} \left(d_x+\frac{d_\theta}{N}\right). \]

At one step, division of the forcing by \(N\) gives \(6\gamma^2L^2(d_x+d_\theta/N)\). The law identity transfers these inequalities to every Gaussian recursion realization satisfying the same input assumptions.

For fixed latent dimension, its contribution persists as \(N\) increases, whereas the parameter contribution \(d_\theta/N\) decreases. This interpretation concerns joint entropy divided by particle count. It is neither unscaled parameter entropy nor error about a deterministic optimizer.

sections.title: The parameter-marginal entropy estimate
sections.intro: Projecting both laws by the measurable parameter map decreases their relative entropy. The reference remains the parameter projection of the same coupled Gibbs target. No marginal-density formula or selected maximizing parameter is needed for this consequence.

steps.title: Parameter projection and extended relative entropy
steps.body:
Let \(p_\theta(z)=\theta\) and define \(\mu_k^\theta=(p_\theta)_\#\mu_k\) and \(\Pi_N^\theta=(p_\theta)_\#\Pi_N\). The same continuous measurable projection preserves probability for each law. Data processing gives

\[ \operatorname{KL}(\mu_k^\theta\Vert\Pi_N^\theta) \le\operatorname{KL}(\mu_k\Vert\Pi_N). \]

This measure inequality does not require a formula for the marginal density or concentration about a point. At the density level it is conditional Jensen for \(u\mapsto u\log u\), applied when averaging over latent coordinates. The measure-theoretic statement remains valid without constructing a conditional density explicitly. Both laws must be projected by the same map; finite joint divergence then implies finite parameter divergence.

steps.title: Finite parameter-entropy bounds and particle normalization
steps.body:
Finite joint divergence first implies finite parameter divergence by extended-valued data processing. The finite quantities may then be compared as real numbers. A full bound \(H_k\le B\) gives parameter upper bound \(B\). A normalized bound \(H_k/N\le\overline B\) instead gives

\[ \operatorname{KL}(\mu_k^\theta\Vert\Pi_N^\theta) \le N\overline B. \]

The positive particle-count multiplier is necessary because joint entropy per particle differs from marginal entropy. Concentration about a likelihood maximizer would require an additional argument for \(\Pi_N^\theta\); this result only compares parameter probability laws.

The full joint estimate gives

\[ \operatorname{KL}(\mu_k^\theta\Vert\Pi_N^\theta) \le e^{-\beta\gamma k/N}H_0+\frac{8\gamma ND L^2}{\beta}. \]

For lifted constant \(N\alpha\) its specialization is

\[ \operatorname{KL}(\mu_k^\theta\Vert\Pi_N^\theta) \le N\left[e^{-\alpha\gamma k}\frac{H_0}{N} +\frac{8\gamma L^2}{\alpha}\left(d_x+\frac{d_\theta}{N}\right)\right]. \]

The initial quantity remains \(H_0=\operatorname{KL}(\mu_0\Vert\Pi_N)\). Data processing does not justify replacing it by the smaller projected initial divergence. The conditional interpolation-data corollaries retain their regularity premises, while the finite-initial-entropy theorem gives the same projection consequence using the constructed Gaussian interpolation.

closing: The joint entropy estimate follows from gradient smoothness, the lifted-target logarithmic Sobolev inequality, the positive step restriction, and finite initial joint entropy. Gaussian interpolation proves its analytic regularity and integrability. Exact coordinate and time substitution give the particle constants. Division by particle count gives the normalized joint estimate; measurable data processing gives the unnormalized parameter-law consequence with the full initial joint entropy retained. The conditional interpolation-data theorems remain valid with their stated additional premises.
